tur69-0: It shows up as pain in the jaw joint just in front of the ear (the temporomandibular joint) and in the chewing muscles, limited mouth opening and jaw noises. In studies based on examination, about one in three adults has a jaw joint disorder (most often disc displacement); symptoms usually settle with simple measures, exercise and physiotherapy.

tur69-2: A clinical guideline published in the BMJ in 2023 strongly recommends cognitive behavioural therapy (alone or combined with relaxation techniques or biofeedback), therapist-assisted jaw mobilisation and manual trigger point therapy, and supervised postural and jaw exercises. It makes a weak recommendation against relaxation techniques used on their own. It strongly recommends against splints that permanently change the bite and against surgery to remove the joint disc.

tur69-4: Based on current evidence, no: exercise has not been shown to slow or stop the progression of dementia. The Cochrane review found no clear benefit for memory and thinking. Even so, exercise may help maintain the ability to carry out daily activities and supports strength, balance, sleep and mood. In a 2026 study (rrAD) that followed 513 people at risk but without dementia for two years, there was no clear difference in thinking and memory tests between those who did aerobic exercise and those who did not. In a review covering more than 4.2 million people, dementia risk was 24% lower in those who were more active in their leisure time than in the least active; these are observational studies.

tur69-7: Reduction in the rate of falls with balance and functional exercises (Cochrane; 39 studies, 7,920 people)
tur69-8: Yes. In a Cochrane review of 108 randomised controlled trials and 23,407 people, exercise reduced the rate of falls in older people living in the community by 23% and the number of people who fell by 15% (high-certainty evidence). Balance and functional exercises reduced the rate of falls by 24% and the number of people who fell by 13% (high-certainty evidence for the rate of falls); programmes that most often combined balance and strengthening reduced them by 34% and 22% (moderate-certainty evidence). In an analysis of 7 studies of the Otago programme on which this page is based (1,503 people, mean age 81.6), falls were reduced by 32%.
